"Shouting fire in a crowded theater" is a misquote that refers to Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr.'s opinion in the United States Supreme Court case Schenck v. United States in 1919 and that is used to express the limits upon which free speech may be expressed under the terms of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution.

Holmes, writing for a unanimous majority, ruled that it was illegal to distribute fliers opposing the draft during World War I. Holmes argued this abridgment of free speech was permissible because it presented a "clear and present danger" to the government's recruitment efforts for the war. Holmes wrote:

The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theater and causing a panic. [...] The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent.

Holmes wrote of falsely shouting fire, because, of course, if there were a fire in a crowded theater, one may rightly indeed shout "Fire!". Falsely shouting "Fire!" in a crowded theater, i.e. shouting "Fire!" when one believes there to be no fire in order to cause panic, was interpreted not to be protected by the First Amendment.

Schenck was later overturned by Brandenburg v. Ohio, which ruled that speech could only be banned when it was directed to and likely to incite imminent lawless action (e.g. a riot), the test which remains until this day. Some now see the Schenck argument to be mistaken, contending that the pamphleteer's actions were more like yelling fire outside a building to prevent people from entering, rather than trying to encourage people to stampede out.

Despite Schenck being overturned, the phrase "shouting fire in a crowded theater" has since come to be known as synonymous with an action that the speaker believes goes beyond the rights guaranteed by free speech, reckless or malicious speech, or an action whose outcomes are blatantly obvious.

Read more: http://www.justanswer.com/law/12gb7-law-not-yelling-fire-public-place.html#ixzz3uxs09Xd2

By ABBAS RANA | Published: Monday, 12/21/2015 12:00 am EST

If the Senate leadership fails to adopt resolutions passed by 40 Senators to modernize the Red Chamber’s inner workings, some Senators from both caucuses may get frustrated and choose to sit as Independents, say organizers of the modernization sessions.

“You may find people who may split from their caucus if they’re disappointed,” said Quebec Liberal Sen. Paul Massicotte in an interview with The Hill Times.

Nova Scotia Conservative Sen. Stephen Greene, co-host of the working sessions in late October to come up with ideas to modernize the Senate, confirmed to The Hill Times that if the Senate fails to implement the modernization ideas, some Senators may choose to sit as Independents.

“There are Senators who are quite restive, I think. So I guess anything could happen,” said Sen. Greene.

Both, however, denied that they had any plans to quit their caucuses, even if they were disappointed with their leaderships for failing to implement the suggested changes.

“I’ll be disappointed if they don’t get adopted but not enough to quit my caucus. I’ll be really disappointed,” said Sen. Massicotte.

Sen. Massicotte and Sen. Greene, with assistance from British Columbia Liberal Sen. Larry Campbell and Alberta Conservative Sen. Scott Tannas, organized a three-day, closed-door working session with about 40 Conservative, Liberal and Independent senators on Parliament Hill from Oct. 26 to Oct. 28, to come up with ideas on Senate modernization. Before that, Sen. Massicotte and Sen. Greene sent out a detailed survey to all Senators to seek ideas on how to improve the inner workings of the Red Chamber.

As a result, the Senators who participated in the working sessions and the survey approved 11 resolutions to modernize the Senate.

Sen. Massicotte and Sen. Greene declined to share the names of Senators who took part in their initiative because all were promised anonymity so that they could speak their minds.

Sen. Massicotte briefed his caucus on the resolutions that came out of the working sessions. He told The Hill Times the overall response from Liberal Senators appeared to be positive. Sen. Greene also briefed his caucus before Parliament adjourned for Christmas break but was not able to cover all the resolutions in his briefing. When Parliament returns in January, he will hold another briefing for his Senate caucus to cover the remainder.

On Dec. 11, both Senators released the details of the working sessions and Sen. Massicotte gave a speech in the Senate Chamber urging his colleagues and the leadership to adopt the proposed changes at the earliest.

“In spite of possible minority opposition, I urge our Senate leaders to undertake the necessary steps to formally have the Senate approve and implement most, if not all, of these recommendations. There is no reason to further delay or to subject these recommendations to further committee study,” said Sen. Massicotte, in his speech.

“For far too long, we have remained inactive and we have let ourselves, our government but foremost, we have let Canadians down when faced with difficult and pressing issues. Our inability to address these concerns has greatly compromised the reputation and legitimacy of this Chamber.”

Some of the 11 resolutions that came out of the working sessions on Senate modernization and the survey include electing chairs, vice-chairs and other members of standing committees; replacing Question Period with Issues Period; electing all caucus officers; televising and webcasting Senate proceedings; a larger communications budget to promote the Senate standing Committee reports; and electing the Speaker.

In the last two months, two Conservative Senators—New Brunswick’s John Wallace and Quebec’s Jacques Demers—resigned from their caucus to sit as Independents, chiefly because of their leadership’s reluctance to reform the inner workings of the Senate and the whipping of votes.

“Differences that I consider to be irreconcilable exist between myself and Conservative Senate Leader Claude Carignan and other Conservative Senate caucus members regarding the required constitutional roles, responsibilities and independence of Conservative senators,” Sen. Wallace wrote in a letter made public in November, explaining his reasons for splitting from the caucus.

“These differences are fundamental to the roles and responsibilities that I have sworn to uphold as a member of the Senate of Canada.”

At present, there are 45 Conservative Senators, 29 Liberals, and nine Independents in the Senate, with 22 vacant seats.

Prime Minister Justin Trudeau (Papineau, Que.) has announced that his government will fill all vacant seats with Independent senators using a “non-partisan, merit based” process, on the advice of an advisory board. In the first phase, five Senators will be appointed early next year, and one of them will hold the position of government Senate representative. It’s unclear, however, how that role will differ from the traditional government Senate leader, which was in place up until the last election.

With the appointment of 22 new Senators, independent Senators would outnumber Liberals.

Sen. Wallace said in his speech that Senate reform in the coming months is inevitable but it’s up to the leadership of the two caucuses whether they want to make the necessary changes on their own or let the new crop of Independent Senators do it.

“Faced with the reality of the numbers of Independent Senators that we will have in this Chamber in the very near future, even if there’s reluctance about what you suggested, the numbers and the presence of these Independent Senators will force change,” Sen. Wallace said in a speech in the Chamber on Dec. 9. “I think the issue is whether leadership is prepared to get out in front of that change and direct it to satisfactory ends and solve real issues, or whether we will move forward kicking and screaming.”

It remains to be seen how many, if any, of the resolutions for modernization will be adopted as some of these would deprive the leadership of their powers that they had been enjoying for decades.

For example, the assignment of committee membership and chair and vice-chairs is controlled, largely, by the leadership of both parties and is a tool to control caucus members.

The replacement of Senate Question Period with Issues Period is also one of the proposals to watch. According to the proposal that came out of the Massicotte-Greene initiative, Senators should focus on issues related to standing committee work and committee reports in Issues Period.

Up until the last Parliament, the government Senate leader, appointed by the prime minister of the day, had answered questions from Senators on behalf of the government.

For Conservative Senators from Atlantic Canada, Senate Question Period is critical, especially after the Liberal sweep of the Atlantic provinces in the House of Commons.

Newfoundland and Labrador Conservative Sen. David Wells told The Hill Times that the Senate Question Period is the only way for Atlantic Canadians to hold the Trudeau government to account.

“I find that discomforting for sure,” said Sen. Wells about the Trudeau government’s decision not to appoint a government Senate leader.

Conservative Senate Leader Claude Carignan declined an interview request for this article but Liberal Senate Leader James Cowan (Halifax, N.S.) told The Hill Times that he put forward a motion in the Senate, two weeks ago, to establish a special committee to look into proposals that came out of the Massicotte-Greene working sessions as well as others that have been put forward in the past. He said that the committee would start its work when Parliament returns for its winter session. Sen. Cowan declined to offer a clear answer about whether he supports the resolutions that have been put forward by the Massicotte-Greene initiative.

“The Senate has decided they’re going to set up a special committee, which I think is the right way to go. You need to have some structure to take these things. We can have groups that meet and arrive at conclusions but unless somebody takes that and actually implements them, they don’t go anywhere. That’s the reason for the special committee. Sen. Carignan supported my motion and it was unanimously adopted,” said Sen. Cowan.

Meanwhile, former Senate Ethics office Jean Fournier, in an interview with The Hill Times, said that in the wake of the Senate expenses scandal that damaged the reputation of the Upper Chamber, Senators also must take strong action to improve the Senate administration’s work, in addition to modernizing the inner workings of the Senate.

“I am specifically referring to finance, administration, and personnel systems, residency requirements and conflict of interest rules. Only then can Senators hope to earn back the confidence of Canadians after the most recent scandals,” said Mr. Fournier

1 And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed. 2 (And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.) 3 And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city. - Luke 2:1-3 (KJV)

 The Christmas Story continues. It is so amazing that God uses even heathen Kings to cause His prophecies to come to past, as it was prophesized that Jesus was to be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). Caesar Augustus ordering that all should be taxed helped fulfill this prophecy. The Jews were at this time living under the rule of the Romans, as they had been conquered by them, so they were having to abide by this decree to be taxed.

 This was not the first time of them being taxed, as this verse shows, but this was at the time so that Mary would deliver Jesus during this trip, fulfilling the prophecy.

 Joseph was a descendant of David’s (Matthew 1:1-17), so he had to take Mary, his wife, and they went to the city of David to register, and pay, the tax that was ordered. The Roman’s were the rulers, and they didn’t care that Mary was about to deliver her first child, but Joseph and Mary had to abide by this decree. The Romans were rulers of the whole known world at this time, so everyone had to go to their ancestral city to be taxed. Can you imagine what confusion such a large amount of people traveling at one time caused, and the hardships that they must have encountered in doing so. Praise God we don’t have to do this in our day and time.
